text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on March 27 in history:
1378 - Pope Gregory XI died. Pope from 1370, in 1377 he restored the Papacy to Rome despite opposition from France.
1625 - King James I of Great Britain died. He was the first Stuart king of England and also the first king to rule both England and Scotland. He was succeeded by Charles I.
1770 - Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, the last great Venetian painter, died.
1785 - Louis XVII, son of King Louis XVI and Queen Marie-Antoinette, born. He was titular king of France from 1793 until his death in 1795.
1794 - The U.S. Navy was officially authorised by Congress.
1802 - Britain, France, Spain and the Batavian Republic signed the Treaty of Amiens, by which England retained Trinidad (taken from Spain) and Ceylon (taken from the Dutch).
1809 - Baron Georges-Eugene Haussmann, French financier and replanner of Paris during the Second Empire, born.
1845 - German scientist Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen born. He received the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901 for his discovery of X-rays.
1878 - Sir George Gilbert Scott, English architect, died. His designs include the Albert memorial in Hyde Park, London.
1889 - John Bright, British statesmen and reformer, died. He worked with Richard Cobden to repeal the Corn Laws.
1912 - James Callaghan, British statesman and Labour prime minister from 1976-1979, born.
1917 - Cyrus Vance, U.S. politician and secretary of state from 1977-80, born.
1923 - Sir James Dewar, Scottish chemist and physicist, died. His inventions include the thermos flask and cordite.

1927 - Mstislav Rostropovich, Russian cellist and conductor, born. One of the world's great cellists, he spent more than 15 years in exile from his native Soviet Union, 11 of them as a stateless citizen.
1933 - Japan announced it would leave the League of Nations after being foung guilty of aggression in Manchuria.
1941 - Prince Paul of Yugoslavia was deposed in a coup d'etat following his pact with Adolf Hitler. The last king of Yugoslavia, Peter II, ruled for a few weeks until Axis troops invaded.
1945 - Germany launched its last V2 rocket from the Hague in the Netherlands, crashing in Orpington, southeast of London. During the war, 8,958 people died in V2 rocket attacks.
1945 - Argentina declared war on Germany and Japan.
1958 - Nikita Krushchev removed Nikolai Bulganin as prime minister and assumed the post himself.
1968 - Yuri Gagarin, first man in space in 1961, was killed in a plane crash near Moscow.
1969 - In Paris peace talks on Vietnam, the North Vietnamese delegate rejected South Vietnam's President Thieu's proposal for direct and secret talks.
1975 - Sir Arthur Bliss, English composer and Master of the Queen's Music, died.

1977 - The world's worst aircraft disaster occurred when two Boeing 747s, owned by KLM and Pan-Am, collided and burst into flames on the runway at Tenerife in the Canary Islands; 583 people were killed out of a total of 644 on board both aircraft.
1980 - 147 people died when the Alexander Kielland, a floating platform for off-duty oil workers, capsized in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea.
1981 - The Soviet Union issued a statement attacking the Polish trade union Solidarity as counter-revolutionary.

1989 - Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, leading a new wave of militancy in Iran's 10-year-old Islamic revolution, prompted the resignation of his moderate successor-designate, Ayatollah Hossein Ali Montazeri.
1994 - Media mogul Silvio Berlusconi seized victory in Italy's general elections, riding a wave of disgust at the country's graft-stained past.
1994 - The Eurofighter, a four-nation project to develop a high-tech fighter jet for Europe's defence, made a successful maiden flight.
1996 - The European Commission banned the sale of British beef and cattle to the rest of the world but tried to ease London's pain with an offer of help for its battered industry.
1996 - Yigal Amir received a life sentence for assassinating Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin in November 1995.
